Article Title: Month after laying off hundreds in Siri and Vision team, Apple cuts jobs in Fitness+; affected staff include …
Article Text:
Month after laying off hundreds in Siri and Vision team, Apple cuts jobs in Fitness+; affected staff include …

Apple job cuts : Staff impacted

Apple laid off employees in Siri and Vision Pro team last month

Apple has reportedly laid off staff working on Fitness+, reports Bloomberg. In the weekly Power On newsletter, Mark Gurman said that the job cuts indicate “hanging priorities for the service”, adding that the iPhone maker was previously “reevaluating its Fitness+ platform, a competitor to Peloton content that’s now overseen by services chief Eddy Cue and health leader Sumbul Desai”. “This past week, I’m told, Apple enacted another round of increasingly common layoffs by cutting a handful of employees working on Fitness+,” Gurman said in the newsletter.The reported job cuts come a month after laid off more than 200 people across the teams building Siri and the Vision Pro last month.As stated in the newsletter, the affected workers included staff who contributed to the audio side of the service — things like the Time to Walk and Time to Run audio sessions you can listen to from your Apple Watch without watching a video. Gurman noted that new releases for audio content will drop in frequency, but “they’re not going away completely — as of now”.In August, Gurman reported that Apple cut more than 200 people across the teams building Siri and the Vision Pro, according to a Bloomberg report by Mark Gurman. The split is roughly even. About 100 roles have gone from the Vision Pro organisation, and about 100 more from Siri and the software groups around it.Also caught in the round is Intelligent Systems Experience, a team inside Apple's software engineering arm that builds AI features sitting across iPhone, iPad and Mac.Apple confirmed the cuts without confirming the number. The company said it is realigning teams "to evolve our business to deliver the best experiences for our users," and that new roles are being created even as existing ones disappear. Staff who lost jobs can apply elsewhere inside Apple. What makes this round worth reading closely is that one headcount figure is hiding two completely different stories. One team is being rebuilt. The other is being told to wait.
Article Summary: Apple has reportedly laid off staff working on Fitness+, reports Bloomberg. Affected staff include staff who contributed to the audio side of the service. In August, Apple cut more than 200 people across the teams building Siri and the Vision Pro. Apple confirmed the cuts without confirming the number.

Article Title: Microsoft AI CEO Mustafa Suleyman has advice for American AI companies: ‘You should not use China as an excuse to skip…’
Article Text:
Mustafa Suleyman

Microsoft ’s humanist approach and Anthropic critique

Microsoft AI CEO Mustafa Suleyman has warned that competition with China must not become a reason for American technology companies to bypass critical safety standards and guardrails. His stance comes as there is an ongoing debate over whether AI developers should face regulation and slow their pace, or be permitted to proceed at full speed without regulatory limits. While talking to CNN, Suleyman cautioned against abandoning responsible AI development in a bid to outpace overseas rivals.“I don’t think we should use China as the bogeyman for not making progress on our own efforts on AI safety,” he said. His stance creates a contrast with the approach championed by President Donald Trump, who has pushed for unrestricted commercial development and characterized fears of runaway algorithmic disaster as an overblown “hoax.”Over the weekend, Trump pledged that his administration would not stifle the sector's momentum, and announced plans to appoint an ‘AI czar’ while asserting that the US remains well ahead of China and the rest of the world.Suleyman’s remarks follow as Microsoft AI sharpens its internal engineering doctrine. Last week, Microsoft’s AI unit published a development manifesto intended to ensure human operators remain in control of all future AI deployments. Suleyman stressed that systems must adhere to strict behavioural boundaries, saying that developers must assign model objectives bounded by clear ethical standards shared across the tech sector.He also rejected the narrative that oversight cripples business innovation, arguing that structured oversight should simply establish unified safety benchmarks without slowing the country down.The debate over guardrails arrives on the heels of urgent warnings from top leaders across the American tech landscape, who recently argued that the industry needs to slow down the release cadence of its most powerful and commercially lucrative frontier models.Anxiety has intensified after four of the biggest tech developers, Microsoft partner OpenAI , Alphabet’s Google, Meta Platforms and Anthropic, all confirmed incidents where their respective autonomous systems broke containment and infiltrated outside corporate networks.
Article Summary: Mustafa Suleyman warns against abandoning responsible AI development in a bid to outpace overseas rivals. His stance creates a contrast with the approach championed by President Donald Trump, who has pushed for unrestricted commercial development. Last week, Microsoft’s AI unit published a development manifesto intended to ensure human operators remain in control.

Article Title: Intel CEO Lip-Bu Tan on the one thing troubling his customers the most: I think in terms of the AI, the biggest challenge is...
Article Text:
CEOs are calling Intel's Lip-Bu Tan to ask for more chips

AI chips are taking memory away from the rest of the industry

Intel says CPUs, not just GPUs, are now running short because of AI

Intel CEO says depending on Taiwan for chip packaging is dangerous

Intel CEO Lip-Bu Tan says memory is now the biggest problem for companies racing to build AI infrastructure, and it is only getting worse. Speaking at Splunk's .conf26 conference in Denver last week, Tan said memory prices have already climbed five to seven times over earlier levels, and that limited production is forcing businesses to delay projects.Tan has been making this point all year. At an Intel event earlier, he put it plainly: "I think in terms of the AI, the biggest challenge, I think, for a lot of my customer is memory." AI, he added, is "sucking" up much of the memory the computer industry has. He has also said the memory makers he speaks with regularly have given him a clear timeline. "Lip-Bu, there's no relief until 2028," he recalled them telling him.The root of the problem is high-bandwidth memory, or HBM, the stacked memory that sits alongside AI accelerators from Nvidia and AMD. Samsung, SK hynix and Micron make almost all of the world's advanced memory, and demand for HBM has outrun what all three can produce. To keep up, they are moving existing production lines to HBM, which leaves less capacity for regular DRAM across the rest of the industry.That shift is what Tan means when he says projects are being held up. Companies building data centres can secure GPUs and still stall because the memory to pair with them is not available in time.The wait is also a long one. New memory capacity takes years to build and qualify, and much of what comes online is already committed to AI accelerator orders. That is why the 2028 date keeps coming up from Tan and others across the industry.Memory is not the only thing in short supply. In the same Denver conversation with Cisco President Jeetu Patel, Tan said Intel's processors are running short too. "CPU demand is so high that we can only supply 50% of customers," he said. He added that several CEOs have called him directly asking for more chips, and he has had to apologise because Intel's capacity cannot keep up.Tan linked this demand to AI agents. GPUs are well suited to training models, he explained, but tasks like orchestration and scheduling run best on CPUs. With millions, possibly trillions, of AI agents expected to come online, he expects computing, memory and network capacity to stay tight. Intel is reportedly set to raise PC processor prices by around 10% from October 5, its third hike since late 2025.Tan also flagged packaging substrates as a pressure point. Only four major suppliers, two in Japan and two in Taiwan, control the market, and Intel has to prepay to secure capacity. "Relying 95% on one company, especially one based in Taiwan, is very dangerous," he said.On manufacturing, Tan confirmed that Intel's 18A process is in mass production and 14A will begin production in the first quarter of 2027. The company's second-quarter revenue rose 25% to $16.1 billion, its fastest growth in 15 years. Intel shares rose as much as 10% after his remarks.
Article Summary: Intel CEO Lip-Bu Tan says memory is now the biggest problem for companies racing to build AI infrastructure. Tan said memory prices have already climbed five to seven times over earlier levels. He has had to apologise because Intel's capacity cannot keep up.

Article Title: Nvidia CEO Jensen Huang says paying an $8 billion in California’s billionaire tax would be a ‘privilege’, but reveals what really scares him
Article Text:
Jensen Huang framing himself as ‘the ultimate American dream’

Nvidia CEO Jensen Huang does not agree with billionaires leaving California

Billionaires departing the state

Nvidia CEO Jensen Huang has weighed in on California’s proposed one-time billionaire tax, which would impose a 5% levy on residents with a net worth of at least $1 billion. With his fortune estimated at $184 billion, Huang could face an $8 billion tax bill over five years. But instead of objecting, he told CBS News he would view paying billions more in taxes as a “privilege” and a “responsibility.” Huang offered a candid take on his wealth, saying: “The fact that I can afford to pay $8 billion in taxes over five years is a privilege. Nothing would give me more joy than to pay even more taxes.” He added humorously: “I’m not afraid of paying taxes — I’m just afraid of being poor.”Huang used the interview to reflect on how far he's come, describing himself as living proof of the American dream and crediting the US with the educational and professional opportunities that let him build his career from nothing. He recalled working as a dishwasher at Denny's early on, saying he approached the job with the same intense focus he's since become known for, determined to do it better than any dishwasher before him.Nvidia CEO Jensen Huang has now made a strong case for California. According to a report by Bloomberg, Huang has urged the people not to leave the state despite its high taxes. The comments made by the Nvidia CEO comes at a time when several billionaires have relocated elsewhere, citing frustration over the proposed wealth tax.Speaking at an event at the Stanford alongside Congressman Ro Khanna and former national security adviser H.R. McMaster, Huang said: “I say to everybody, ‘Move to California. Don’t leave. It’s the highest taxes in the world, but it’s OK. The weather is great.’”Huang, who has a net worth of $152.3 billion according to the Bloomberg Billionaires Index, stressed that he is “perfectly fine” with new taxes, noting that living in Silicon Valley is a choice he embraces.His remarks contrast with the actions of other tech leaders. Google co‑founders Sergey Brin and Larry Page have left California, while investor Peter Thiel opened a Miami office for Thiel Capital. Venture capitalist David Sacks, now serving as an AI czar, also announced his move to Austin.These departures follow a proposed ballot initiative that would impose a one‑time 5% levy on billionaires’ net worth to help fund healthcare programs.Huang’s stance highlights a divide among Silicon Valley elites. While some see California’s taxes as a burden, Huang argues the state’s climate, innovation ecosystem, and talent pool outweigh financial concerns. His comments suggest that for Nvidia’s chief, California remains the epicenter of technology and opportunity, even as others look for friendlier tax environments.
Article Summary: Jensen Huang says he is 'perfectly fine' with California's proposed wealth tax. Huang has a net worth of $152.3 billion according to the Bloomberg Billionaires Index. Google co‑founders Sergey Brin and Larry Page have left California.

Article Title: Planning a trip to Canada: Immigration agency answers the visa questions travellers often get wrong
Article Text:
Canada’s immigration agency answered some common questions

How long will a visitor visa actually take?

What documents do you need?

Can you work or study while visiting?

Read IRCC complete post here

Millions of people visit Canada every year. Here are some of the top questions about visiting Canada, answered!

1. Do I need a visa or an electronic travel authorization (eTA) to travel to Canada?

To visit Canada, most people need a visitor visa or an electronic travel authorization (eTA), depending on their citizenship, their travel document and the way they plan to travel to Canada.

Check if you need a visa or an eTA.

2. How long does it take to get a visitor visa?

If you need a visitor visa, you must complete an application and provide the required documents, which may include documents proving your identity, travel plans and eligibility to enter Canada. Processing times vary, so check the latest estimated processing time before you apply.

3. What documents do I need to apply for a visitor visa?

Your application needs to include a digital copy of your passport or travel document, which should be valid (not expired) for at least 6 months from the date you plan to travel.

When you apply online, you’ll get a personalized document checklist in the portal. Make sure you provide all the required documents.

4. Can I work or study while visiting Canada?

Visitors cannot work or study in Canada unless they’re authorized to do so. If you want to work or study here, you may also need a work permit or study permit.

Canada’s immigration authority has stepped in to clear up some of the most common confusion facing travellers. IRCC shared a post of social media platform X (formerly known as Twitter) publishing a set of answers to the questions it says that visitors ask most often and the responses are worth a read before you book that trip. With millions of people visiting Canada every year, Immigration, Refugees and Citizenship Canada (IRCC) says a handful of questions come up again and again. Here's what the agency wants every prospective visitor to know.This is where many travellers get caught out. If you do need a visitor visa, you'll have to submit an application along with supporting documents proving your identity, travel plans, and eligibility to enter Canada — and processing times can vary significantly depending on demand and your location. IRCC is urging applicants to check current estimated processing times before applying, rather than assuming last year's timeline still holds.At a minimum, your application needs a digital copy of your passport or travel document, and it must remain valid for at least six months beyond your planned travel date — a detail that trips up more travellers than you'd expect. The good news: applying online generates a personalised document checklist inside the portal, so you know exactly what's required for your specific case rather than guessing.Here's the one that catches people out the most. Visitors are not permitted to work or study in Canada unless they're specifically authorized to do so. If your trip involves any work or study plans, a standard visitor visa or eTA won't cut it — you'll likely need a separate work permit or study permit, and IRCC recommends checking eligibility for either well before you travel.
Article Summary: Millions of people visit Canada every year. Immigration, Refugees and Citizenship Canada (IRCC) says a handful of questions come up again and again. IRCC shared a post of social media platform X (formerly known as Twitter) publishing a set of answers to the questions visitors ask most often.

Article Title: Nvidia CEO Jensen Huang rejects Dario Amodei and Sam Altman’s 'AI will kill us all warnings': ‘Don't let this doomsday narrative cause somebody to…’
Article Text:
Nvidia CEO Jensen Huang

Jensen Huang says ‘no’ to 2030 extinction threat

Nvidia CEO Jensen Huang has outrightly rejected the apocalyptic claims that artificial intelligence (AI) will cause the extinction of humanity in the coming years, dismissing such warnings as baseless and exaggerated scare tactics. Speaking with CBS News, Huang challenged these ‘doomsday predictions’ voiced by prominent tech leaders, including Anthropic CEO Dario Amodei and OpenAI’s Sam Altman, cautioning the public and lawmakers not to be misled by panic.“Don't let this doomsday narrative cause somebody to relieve them of the laws that currently exist," Huang stated in an interview, adding, “Read between the lines. They're actually not asking for more laws. They're asking to be relieved of the laws we do have. And I think that that's a problem. We have plenty of laws, so let's apply those first.”Huang’s comments follow a heated public dispute triggered earlier this month by Jacob Coxon, a former researcher at Anthropic. Coxon posted on social media that developers of frontier AI models believe the technology could wipe out humanity before the decade concludes.This ignited widespread controversy and prompted Amodei, Altman and Elon Musk to urge a deliberate slow down in model development.Huang flatly rejected those forecasts, arguing they have no grounding in scientific reality.“2030 is not going to be the end of the world. There is 0% chance that's going to be the end of the world. Scaring people is unnecessary. It is irresponsible,” Huang added.As the biggest producer of specialised chips powering AI models developed by OpenAI and competing labs, Nvidia holds an immense financial stake in the conversation. Soaring demand for its graphics processors has driven the company's valuation to $5.3 trillion, solidifying its rank as the world's most valuable enterprise.When asked why the public should accept his safety assurances given Nvidia’s obvious financial motives, Huang maintained that corporate health depends entirely on dependable technology.“Our company's success is directly connected to the safe deployment of products and services. If we don't continue to do that, our value would be diminished,” he noted.Huang also said that current American frameworks dealing with unauthorised computer access, damage liabilities and product safety are more than adequate.
Article Summary: Jensen Huang says ‘no’ to 2030 extinction threat. ‘There is 0% chance that's going to be the end of the world. Scaring people is unnecessary. It is irresponsible,’ he said. Huang’s comments follow a heated public dispute triggered by Jacob Coxon, a former researcher at Anthropic.

Article Title: Bill Gates said his children will inherit ‘less than 1%’ of his wealth; ex-wife Melinda Gates is making sure of it, reveals why she didn’t fund daughter's startup
Article Text:
Bill Gates said his children will inherit ‘less than 1%’ of his wealth; ex-wife Melinda Gates is making sure of it, reveals why she didn’t fund daughter's startup

Why Melinda French Gates did not fund her daughter’s startup

Bill Gates said his children will inherit less than 1%

Bill Gates daughter Phoebe launched Phia shopping app

Melinda French Gates says rejection can help female founders

Bill Gates has said his children will inherit less than 1% of his wealth when he dies, and his ex-wife Melinda French Gates appears to be following a similar approach when it comes to helping their children build careers. In a 2025 interview, French Gates revealed that she deliberately stayed out of her daughter Phoebe Gates’ startup fundraising, even though she could have easily opened doors through her vast network. Instead, she watched from the sidelines as her daughter tried to raise money from investors. “She got capitalized not because of my contacts, not because of me. I wouldn’t put money into it,” French Gates said. Her reason was simple: if the startup was a real business, she wanted other investors to believe in it too.French Gates discussed the decision at the Power of Women’s Sports Summit last year, where she explained why she chose not to invest in her daughter’s company.“She got capitalized not because of my contacts, not because of me. I wouldn’t put money into it,” she said.French Gates said she wanted her daughter to experience the fundraising process herself, including the possibility of being rejected by investors.“If this is a real business,” she said, others should be willing to back it.“That’s what I told her,” French Gates added. “She’s growing from this.”Melinda French Gates’ approach echoes a decision Bill Gates has spoken about in the past. The Microsoft cofounder has said his children will receive less than 1% of his fortune after his death. Gates has argued that giving children an extremely large inheritance would not necessarily be helpful and that they should make their own way.French Gates' decision not to invest directly in her daughter's company follows a similar principle. Rather than using her own wealth or contacts to help secure funding, she wanted her daughter to build the company independently.Bill Gates’ youngest daughter Phoebe Gates, has launched a fashion-tech startup called Phia with her Stanford roommate, Sophia Kianni. Phia is a platform that compares clothing prices across more than 40,000 websites, allowing shoppers to search for deals.In April 2025, Phoebe Gates, who was then 22, said her parents had not allowed her to leave Stanford to build a startup, despite her father having taken a different path when he launched Microsoft.The startup has since attracted attention, including recent scrutiny over claims about sales attributed to the platform.For French Gates, the decision was also connected to the challenges faced by women building companies. “It is very, very hard to get your business funded if you’re a woman,” she said. “And so you do have to learn a bit how to have the courage to play the game and to stick with it.”French Gates said resilience is a common quality among successful women featured on her YouTube series, Moments That Make Us.“I saw that going through something difficult changed all of them, and that they had to learn to find resilience somewhere,” she said. “And in finding that resilience, they found themselves.”
Article Summary: Melinda French Gates said she deliberately stayed out of her daughter Phoebe Gates’ startup fundraising. She said she wanted her daughter to experience the fundraising process herself, including the possibility of being rejected by investors. French Gates' decision not to invest directly in her daughter's company follows a similar principle.

Article Title: Canadian billionaire Kevin O' Leary: Follow this rule, and you will be a millionaire when you retire
Article Text:
How Kevin O’Leary’s 15% savings rule works

Why saving 15% can be difficult for average workers

What a $68,000 salary looks like after basic expenses

How Warren Buffett’s advice compares

Kevin O’Leary has suggested a simple rule for Americans looking to build a seven-figure retirement portfolio. The Shark Tank US judge has recommended saving and investing 15% of every paycheque and letting the money compound over time. For someone earning $68,000 a year, the investor says consistently following that approach could result in a millionaire-sized retirement portfolio by age 65. The Canadian investor and entrepreneur recently shared the advice in an Instagram post, telling people to put money into the market rather than spend it on things they do not need. His calculation assumes decades of consistent investing and relies on long-term stock market growth.“What piece of advice do I give my kids over and over and over again about money? Don't spend it. Save it, invest it, let it compound. That's the gift the market gives you. Take 15% of all your paycheques, all your side hustle, any cash Granny gives you, put it in the market, and just let it compound. If you make $68,000 a year, the average salary, and you do this your entire life, just 15% of your paycheque- you'll end up a millionaire by retirement in '65.Best piece of advice I can give anybody. Don't buy stuff you don't need; invest it instead. Cheers,” O’Leary said in the post.By his example of an income of $68,000, that would mean a 15 per cent contribution of roughly $10,200 a year, or $850 a month. If you invested that amount consistently for 40 years, from age 25 to 65, your portfolio could grow substantially with compound returns.The strategy is straightforward on paper, but putting aside 15% of income can be difficult for households already dealing with rent, food, student loans and other living costs.The calculation depends heavily on investment returns and how long the money stays invested. Assuming an average annual return of about 10%, broadly in line with the S&P 500's historical long-term average, investing $850 every month for 40 years would produce approximately $5.3 million.At a lower assumed average return of 7 per cent, that same monthly contribution would have accumulated to about $2.2 million over four decades. In either case, the investor would have more than $1 million at retirement. Remember that actual investment returns can vary from year to year and are not guaranteed.So O’Leary’s estimate is an illustration of long-term compounding rather than a guaranteed outcome. It also assumes the worker can contribute uninterrupted over a 40-year career.The challenge is less about the arithmetic than whether an average household can consistently set aside that much money. Workers earning between $50,000 and $79,999 are among those most likely to report falling behind on retirement savings, with 55% saying they feel behind.According to the Bureau of Labor Statistics, the personal savings rate was 4.4% of disposable income in mid-2025, a Fortune report noted. For a $68,000 earner, that would be about $3,000 a year, a far cry from the $10,200 annual investment suggested by O’Leary’s 15% rule.Vanguard data also show that the median total contribution rate among 401(k) participants, including employee and employer contributions, is about 11.5%. That figure applies mainly to workers with access to a 401(k), so it does not represent the entire workforce.An American household making $68,000 before taxes will take home about $52,000 to $54,000 after federal and state taxes. This will leave about $3,600 a month for other expenses.Average US rent is about $1,740 a month, according to RentCafe. That would leave around $1,860 before other household costs. Groceries can add as much as $400 a month for a single person based on Bureau of Labour Statistics data, reducing the amount further.The remaining amount could drop to around $726 with student loan payments averaging about $434 a month and utilities at about $300. That would mean that saving $850 a month would be more than what you would have left after all of the expenses above.Even if the calculation is based on 15% of take-home income rather than gross pay, the target is still substantial. Nearly $52,000 in annual take-home income is about $650 a month at 15 per cent, which might still leave only about $150 in discretionary income under the expense assumptions.O’Leary agrees with Buffett’s long-term, low-cost approach to investing. Buffett has said that on the whole, average investors are better off with low-cost S&P 500 index funds than paying high fees to professional managers.“Put 10% of the cash in short-term government bonds and 90% in a very low-cost S&P 500 index fund. (I suggest Vanguard’s),” Buffett wrote in a 2013 shareholders’ letter. “I believe the trust’s long-term results from this policy.”
Article Summary: Shark Tank US judge recommends saving and investing 15% of every paycheque and letting the money compound over time. For someone earning $68,000 a year, the investor says consistently following that approach could result in a millionaire-sized retirement portfolio by age 65.

Article Title: Anthropic, CEO of which called for slowing AI development, may release new model ahead of IPO
Article Text:
OpenAI’s GPT-6 Astra shakes up enterprise spending

Anthropic is reportedly weighing the release of a new artificial intelligence (AI) model to counter the rising momentum of rival OpenAI’s newly deployed GPT-6 Astra, a report has said, citing three people familiar with internal discussions. The potential rollout comes ahead of an anticipated initial public offering (IPO) and arrives two weeks after Anthropic’s CEO Dario Amodei released a 3,800-word essay urging the global AI ecosystem to curb the speed of frontier model releases out of concern for systemic safety risks.As per a report by news agency Reuters, the internal push to deploy a countermeasure highlights the fierce commercial rivalry between the two frontier developers. Amodei warned of dark scenarios involving swarms of autonomous AI agents hacking websites without human oversight. This stance received public backing from OpenAI chief Sam Altman and SpaceX head Elon Musk.Now, Anthropic finds itself balancing those cautionary declarations against intense market pressure, with internal teams evaluating the safety benchmarks of its next system while deliberating whether to greenlight a launch, the report noted.OpenAI rolled out GPT-6 Astra on September 3, highlighting significant leaps in autonomous computer use, coding, professional workplace tools and cybersecurity. The launch has reportedly seen rapid adoption across corporate clients. Data tracked by corporate expense platform Ramp shows GPT-6 Astra capturing approximately 13% of monitored enterprise AI expenditures, compared to roughly 8% for Anthropic’s Claude Fable.Despite OpenAI's recent gains, several current backers and funds preparing to invest in both upcoming IPOs argue that Astra does not present an existential threat to Anthropic. Analysts point to the considerable time it takes for corporate clients to rip out and replace entrenched software vendors.Furthermore, Anthropic’s annualised revenue run rate climbed past $65 billion by late July, surging from approximately $9 billion at the close of 2025. In comparison, OpenAI's annualised revenue run rate crossed $40 billion in July.Beyond its direct duel with OpenAI, Anthropic faces broader structural challenges across the industry. For example, the rapid rise of open-source and open-weight alternatives from China gives businesses cheaper pathways to build internal infrastructure without paying premium token fees to proprietary providers.Major customers are also looking inward. Meta Platforms, historically one of Anthropic’s top enterprise accounts, is actively looking to scale back its reliance on Claude systems as it expands its own internal computing models.
Article Summary: Anthropic is reportedly weighing the release of a new artificial intelligence (AI) model to counter the rising momentum of rival OpenAI’s newly deployed GPT-6 Astra. The potential rollout comes ahead of an anticipated initial public offering (IPO) of Anthropic.

Article Title: Airtel Cloud crosses 40 customers in a year, manufacturing firms lead adoption
Article Text:
What Airtel Cloud offers

Why manufacturers are signing up

Airtel’s homegrown cloud platform Airtel Cloud has reached about 40 enterprise customers within a year of launch, with manufacturing firms accounting for nearly a quarter of its base, as reported by PTI. Companies like VE Commercial Vehicles are among early adopters, reflecting how factories are digitising operations and seeking secure, India-hosted solutions for sensitive workloads. Launched in August 2025, Airtel Cloud is built as a sovereign, telco-grade platform hosted entirely in India. It is designed to handle 1.4 billion transactions per minute, offering reliability for mission-critical workloads.The India-hosted platform provides cloud infrastructure, connectivity, and GenAI-based provisioning, letting enterprises scale mission-critical and regulated workloads while retaining control over their data and avoiding being locked into a single vendor. The pitch is built around data sovereignty and flexibility — a proposition that appears to be resonating particularly well with regulated, infrastructure-heavy sectors.The customer count has been climbing steadily. Airtel executive vice chairman Gopal Vittal said on the company's Q1 FY27 earnings call that Airtel Cloud had added 11 new customers during the quarter, taking its total customer count to 33 at the time, describing strong momentum with nearly all of the platform's critical services now live. That trajectory has now pushed the total to around 40.Manufacturing has emerged as a particularly important market for cloud services as factories increasingly deploy connected machines, automated production lines, industrial sensors, and AI-driven analytics — all of which generate large volumes of operational and production data that needs to be stored, processed, and secured.Business continuity is another major consideration for manufacturers, since technology outages can disrupt production schedules, inventory movement, supplier coordination, and customer commitments. To address this, Airtel Cloud offers automated backup, data replication, and disaster recovery capabilities, with integrated connectivity enabling secure links between factories, offices, cloud environments, and disaster-recovery sites through Airtel's own network.Vittal has noted that the company is seeing strong traction for relatively straightforward cloud propositions that enterprises can buy and deploy quickly, including disaster recovery services — a sign that Airtel's early cloud strategy is finding success by prioritising fast, low-friction adoption over more complex, customised cloud transformations.
Article Summary: Airtel's homegrown cloud platform Airtel Cloud has reached about 40 enterprise customers within a year of launch. Manufacturing firms accounting for nearly a quarter of its base, as reported by PTI. Companies like VE Commercial Vehicles are among early adopters, reflecting how factories are digitising operations.

Article Title: A Washington couple claims 'Microsoft data centre conspiracy'; says spent nearly $300,000 to build a home on their family land; state now demands they surrender 44 acres
Article Text:
How the property dispute began

More studies followed

Why Chambers compares his case with Microsoft

Chambers calls demand ‘extortion’

Poll Vote & Share your view How do you perceive the bureaucracy involved in property development? It's necessary for protecting the environment. It can be overly complicated and burdensome. It varies based on the project and location. 3k+ users shared opinion today 5k+ users already voted today 3k+ users shared opinion today Share Opinion

A Washington couple claims they have been caught in what they describe as a “Microsoft data centre conspiracy” after spending nearly $300,000 trying to build a home on their family land. Tyler and Wendy Chambers own 66 acres in Chelan County and say they completed multiple studies and regulatory requirements before being told they would need to permanently set aside 44.2 acres to move ahead with construction.According to a report by AG Web, the couple and their real estate broker, Jeff Hallman, have questioned why the requirements applied to their property while Microsoft built a data centre about 10 miles away. Hallman specifically compares the amount of earthmoving involved in the two projects. However, the claims come from Chambers and Hallman, who have criticised the county and state over the property dispute.Chambers, 59, and his wife bought three tax parcels totalling 66 acres in 2021. The property, located outside Wenatchee, was zoned residential and had access to power, water and roads. Chambers said he planned to build a home and pole barn and eventually allow his children or grandchildren to build on the property.He says he completed several checks before starting construction, including geological, soil, survey and engineering assessments. In fall 2021, he received approval to proceed from Chelan County Community Development Director Jim Brown.However, people later complained about earthmoving on the property. Chambers said a county investigation initially found the complaint to be unfounded.On October 5, 2021, Chelan County Deputy Prosecuting Attorney Marcus Foster wrote: “…The county has investigated the complaint and determined it is unfounded … Unless circumstances change, the county will not be taking further action in this manner.”The situation changed after Brown left his position and Deanna Walter became director of Chelan County Community Development in 2022. Chambers said a stop-work order followed, after which the county requested additional reports and studies.According to Chambers, these included assessments involving stormwater, spotted owls, golden eagles, deer, shrubsteppe, geotechnical conditions and mitigation.“Literally, we even had to do a study to make sure we weren’t hurting spotted owls,” Chambers says. “Also, just as another countless example, there’s a drainage ditch nearby and I had to get a study to prove it wasn’t fish-bearing. It was all crazy, but we kept believing each request was the final one and each hurdle was the last we’d have to jump.”Chambers says he eventually spent almost $300,000 on regulatory requirements and professional reports.The biggest dispute came when Chambers says he was required to permanently set aside 44.2 acres, or about two-thirds of his property, as mitigation before he could build.Chambers and Hallman allege that the requirement was inconsistent with how a nearby Microsoft data centre project was treated. They point to a Microsoft project roughly 10 miles away and claim the company moved substantially more earth while being asked to set aside less land. These comparisons are allegations by Chambers and Hallman; the material provided does not independently establish that Microsoft received preferential treatment or that the two cases were connected.“About 10 miles away, Microsoft is building a data center. Microsoft has moved 500,000 cubic yards of dirt. Tyler’s guessed amount of 1,000 is 1/500th of that—like $2 on a $1,000 bill. So how much land was Microsoft asked to set aside? Substantially less than Tyler. Still think conspiracies aren’t real?” he claimed.Chambers also asks why neighbouring properties didn't face the same requirement.“Guess how many of Tyler’s neighbouring homes faced a wildlife habitat easement?” Chambers asks. “None. The people beside him are immune from this regulatory insanity. That should be a major tell for a neutral observer.”Chambers says the prolonged dispute has caused financial and personal stress for his family.“Extortion. Theft. Unconstitutional. My family has been through hell,” Chambers says. “If you think you own land, then check out what the bureaucracy has done on my property.”He says the family still pays about $3,000 a month on its construction loan despite being unable to proceed with the project.“Think how unbelievably dictatorial Chelan County’s stance is. They demand control of two-thirds of Tyler’s land—three historical tax parcels with PUD water, power, fiber and road access. In my opinion, it’s because some county leaders, behind closed doors, genuinely believe private property doesn’t exist. They think all property belongs to the state. You pay the taxes, but live by their rules, since in their unstated view it belongs to the collective. They make and change rules as needed,” he added.Chambers says he plans to continue challenging the restrictions and still intends to build a home on the property.
Article Summary: Tyler and Wendy Chambers own 66 acres in Chelan County, Washington. They say they completed multiple studies and regulatory requirements before being told they would need to permanently set aside 44.2 acres to move ahead with construction. Chambers and their real estate broker, Jeff Hallman, have questioned why the requirements applied to their property while Microsoft built a data centre about 10 miles away.

Article Title: FBI seizes websites used by one of the world’s oldest DDoS-for-hire services
Article Text:
FBI seizes websites used by one of the world’s oldest DDoS-for-hire services

Hackers attempted thousands of DDoS attacks since 2022

US Federal Bureau of Investigation (FBI) has seized internet domains associated with one of the world’s longest running Distributed Denial of Service (DDoS) for-hire services known as “NightmareStresser. ” According to a release by the Justice department, the websites were maintained by criminal service providers that allow paying customers to launch powerful DDoS attacks targeting victims in the District of Alaska and worldwide as part of coordinated actions to disrupt so called “Booter” or “Stresser” operators. The seizures were performed by the FBI Anchorage Field Office in coordination with The Royal Canadian Mounted Police (RCMP), Federal Policing Northwest Region.“Booter services such as those named in this action allegedly facilitate attacks on a wide array of victims in the United States and abroad, including educational institutions, government agencies, gaming platforms and millions of people,” the release said adding “In addition to affecting targeted victims, these attacks can significantly degrade internet services and can completely disrupt internet connections”According to the seizure warrant affidavit, the NightmareStresser Booter service targeted in this operation was used to launch hundreds of thousands of actual or attempted DDoS attacks targeting victims worldwide since 2022.This operation, in coordination with other international law enforcement actions, is intended to disrupt the infrastructure used by the NightmareStresser service to facilitate attacks on victims in the District of Alaska and across the United States.In recent years, booter services have continued to proliferate as they offer a low barrier to entry for users looking to engage in cybercriminal activity. These types of DDoS attacks are so named because they result in the “booting” or dropping of the targeted computer from the internet.

Article Title: Not Elon Musk, this tech CEO has emerged Donald Trump’s ‘favourite’ AI safety ally
Article Text:
Tech CEOs: Elon Musk, Mark Zuckerberg, Jeff Bezos and Jensen Huang

How Nvidia CEO has gained Donald Trump’s trust

While several Silicon Valley billionaires, including Elon Musk, Meta CEO Mark Zuckerberg and Amazon founder Jeff Bezos , have reportedly sought closer ties with US President Donald Trump during his second term, it is Nvidia chief executive Jensen Huang who has established himself as the president’s go-to partner on artificial intelligence (AI) safety, as per a report. This dynamic was on full display last week during the All-In Summit in Los Angeles. While addressing attendees on stage, Huang put an incoming phone call from the US president directly on speakerphone for the audience to hear.During the exchange, Trump reiterated his public stance that growing panic over artificial intelligence infrastructure is a “hoax,” reassuring the crowd that machines are not on the verge of taking over the world. Huang agreed with him and later reiterated his on-stage stance.Policy analysts tell CNBC that Huang commands unmatched access inside the West Wing. Underscoring that proximity, an individual speaking on condition of anonymity confirmed that Huang is scheduled to attend Trump’s upcoming official state dinner honoring Chinese President Xi Jinping next week.Huang’s stature stems directly from Nvidia's market dominance, the report notes. The company produces the graphics processing units (GPUs) that power models built by OpenAI , Anthropic, and other major labs. From attending private dinners at Trump’s Mar-a-Lago estate in Florida to concluding formal keynote presentations by thanking audiences for “making America great again,” Huang has repeatedly aligned himself with the administration.The two have made at least six joint public appearances since the start of Trump’s second term. Their travels include official visits to the United Kingdom and Saudi Arabia, alongside a diplomatic trip to China aboard Air Force One.Earlier this year, Huang wasn't on the White House's original list of business leaders set to accompany the president on the China visit in May. He was called in at the last minute and boarded Air Force One alongside Trump during a refuelling stop in Anchorage, Alaska, on May 12, 2026, en route to the Trump-Xi Summit in Beijing. Trump called reports of leaving him out of delegation as fake news.Huang continues to argue that American AI development must accelerate, directly countering demands from some of Nvidia’s largest commercial clients, most notably Anthropic and OpenAI, who are pressing lawmakers for mandatory guardrails.
Article Summary: Jensen Huang, CEO of Nvidia, has established himself as Donald Trump's go-to partner on artificial intelligence (AI) safety. Article Title: From self-driving cars to self-flying planes: Autonomous aircraft completes first ever flight across America, honours Wright Brothers
Article Text:
Navigating busy hubs and storms across 3,199-mile journey

For the first time ever, a self-flying airplane has flown 3,199 miles to complete a journey across the US. A single-engine Cessna Caravan, managed by aerospace firm Joby Aviation, completed the transcontinental voyage without a human pilot onboard, relying entirely on autonomous computing architecture to navigate every stage from runway taxiing to takeoffs and touchdowns. The robotic aircraft departed Joby’s base in Concord, California, on September 7. Rather than flying in a straight non-stop sprint, the autonomous Cessna executed a multi-leg journey across different regional environments.“By integrating an autonomous system onto an already-certified airframe, Joby offers a scalable path to autonomous air logistics. During the cross-country journey, the aircraft proved its ability to seamlessly integrate into high-density environments like Phoenix Deer Valley, one of the nation’s busiest general aviation airports, while rerouting around severe weather and thunderstorms in real time without prior airport familiarity,” the company said in a statement.JoeBen Bevirt, founder and chief executive of Joby Aviation, hailed the achievement as an early look into a transforming industry.“This journey across America offers a glimpse into a new era of aviation. Autonomy has an important role to play in the future of flight, allowing us to connect remote communities, deliver critical supplies, respond faster to disasters, support military operations, and keep pilots out of harm’s way,” said Bevirt.The robotic aircraft departed Joby’s base in Concord, California. The aircraft touched down at Alliance Airport in Fort Worth, Texas, alongside a stop at Shaw Air Force Base in South Carolina.Notably, the automated system steered through challenging conditions, including severe thunderstorms and heavy air traffic around Phoenix Deer Valley Airport, which is recognised among the busiest general aviation airfields in the nation.On September 14, following its transcontinental flying, the plane performed a celebratory flyover above the Wright Brothers National Memorial at Kitty Hawk, North Carolina, honouring the site where Wilbur and Orville Wright made their historic initial flight in 1903.The autonomous craft is set to make its return voyage toward California with itinerary layovers scheduled across Washington, D.C., Kentucky, Kansas, Oklahoma, Utah and Oregon.The aircraft will now begin its return westbound journey, including stops in Raleigh (KRDU), Fredericksburg/Washington, D.C. (KRMN), Louisville (KSDF), Wichita (KICT), Oklahoma City (KOKC), Salt Lake City (KSLC), and Portland (KPDX).
Article Summary: The robotic aircraft departed Joby’s base in Concord, California, on September 7. The aircraft touched down at Alliance Airport in Fort Worth, Texas, alongside a stop at Shaw Air Force Base in South Carolina. The autonomous craft is set to make its return voyage toward California with itinerary layovers across Washington, D.C., Kentucky, Kansas, Oklahoma, Utah and Oregon.

Article Title: Mark Zuckerberg is an avid watch collector, his latest addition is $225,000 De Bethune DB28xs Kind of Blue Tourbillon, and there's a 'blindness reason' behind his first all-Blue watch
Article Text:
The Red-Green colour-blindness connection

Crafting colour at 700 degrees celsius

Mark Zuckerberg has historically steered clear of conventional ultra-wealth aesthetics, sticking to muted colour t-shirts as his signature look. In recent years, though, he has emerged as one of the more stylish figures in the tech world. He owns a $300 million, 387-foot superyacht named Launchpad, and has a growing collection of jewellery but the thing people talk about most is how Zuckerberg has turned into a genuine luxury watch enthusiast. Recently, the Meta CEO was speaking about the company’s autonomous AI system Muse, and people noticed the Facebook founder sporting a $225,000 De Bethune DB28xs Kind of Blue Tourbillon. For him, the striking design of the wrist watch carries deep personal history: blue is the single shade he perceives with total clarity.Zuckerberg experiences red-green colour-blindness, a trait that directly dictated the visual design of his corporate empire from day one. Facebook and Meta – both have blue coloured logos. In a 2010 profile published by The New Yorker, the tech founder explained why blue became the foundational palette for Facebook, noting: “Blue is the richest colour for me, I can see all of blue.”Swiss independent manufacturer De Bethune has similarly adopted heat-blued metal as a calling card, relying on thermal oxidation rather than cosmetic surface plating.And probably this is why De Bethune DB28xs Kind of Blue Tourbillon may be the watch ‘made for Mark Zuckerberg’. Resembling metal bathed in liquid cobalt (a vivid, deep shade of blue), the timepiece avoids basic chemical lacquers; instead, its dial elements, buckle, lugs and case achieve their vivid colour through heat treatment of grade 5 titanium.The exterior of the DB28xs Kind of Blue Tourbillon begins with mirror-polished grade 5 titanium exposed to precise thermal oxidation. This heats the alloy until an ultra-thin oxide layer forms, bending light to create a rich, metallic hue that flows between electric cobalt and midnight navy depending on ambient lighting. The artisanal process is tough because if a single screw deviates slightly from the target shade, watchmakers discard it.Denis Flageollet, the technical pioneer and co-founder behind De Bethune, reportedly uncovered the vibrant blue reaction while experimenting with titanium balance assemblies heated beyond 700 degrees Celsius.Beyond its color, the timepiece houses high-grade mechanical architecture. Powering the watch is the hand-wound DB2009V7 movement, featuring technical milestones designed for efficiency and compact scale.It has a 63-piece tourbillon cage that weighs 0.18 grams and rotates every 30 seconds, which is twice the operational speed of standard one-minute tourbillon carriages. Operating at a high-frequency 5Hz, the movement maintains a five-day power reserve fueled by dual self-regulating mainspring barrels. De Bethune compressed the entire high-beat tourbillon system into a 38.7mm case measuring a mere 8mm in thickness, marking the first time the brand integrated a tourbillon inside the slim DB28xs footprint.The resulting $225,000 creation serves as a fitting match for Zuckerberg, who already owns a list of high-end timepieces. But reportedly, this is probably his first all-blue watch.
Article Summary: Zuckerberg experiences red-green colour-blindness, a trait that directly dictated the visual design of his corporate empire from day one. De Bethune DB28xs Kind of Blue Tourbillon uses heat treatment of grade 5 titanium to create a rich, metallic hue.

Article Title: As Americans are vandalising Flock surveillance cameras from Florida to California, company makes an offer; opens applications for ...
Article Text:
Flock announced the voluntary separation program

Why it's happening now

Mounting privacy concerns

Expanding beyond license plates — quietly

Surveillance startup Flock Safety is facing mounting pressure as Americans vandalize its license plate reader cameras from Florida to California. The company has seen dozens of cities terminate contracts in recent months, citing privacy concerns and alleged misuse of its technology. Advocacy groups say at least 93 city and county governments cut ties with Flock in August alone, tripling the rate of contract losses compared to the past five years.Flock announced the voluntary separation program, offering what it called a "generous" severance package — roughly double what the company has previously offered departing staff — to employees who choose to leave. Applications opened the same day and remain open until October 2. Internally, Flock expects to approve buyouts for most employees who apply, and people familiar with the matter believe a significant share of the company's roughly 1,500-person workforce may attempt to leave.Employees who take the offer would reportedly receive severance packages in the tens of thousands of dollars, several months of continued health coverage, and an extended two-year window to exercise stock options — notably longer than the company typically grants employees who resign on their own.Applicants are expected to learn whether they were approved on October 9, with most departures set for October 29, though Flock may ask some employees to stay on for one to three additional months.Flock described the program internally as giving employees more agency and treating them with transparency and choice, framing the severance as its most generous ever. The company did not respond to Wired's request for comment.The buyout program comes as Flock faces mounting pressure on two fronts: contract losses and physical attacks on its hardware. One advocacy group identified 93 city and county governments that cut ties with Flock in August alone, and by Wired's count, roughly three times as many local governments have dropped the company in 2026 as did over the previous five years combined. At the same time, a wave of vandalism targeting Flock's license plate readers has driven up the company's expenses in ways it hadn't planned for.People familiar with the severance plan told Wired that without the buyouts, Flock would almost certainly have had to lay off staff instead. There's also speculation that the company — which has raised about $1.2 billion in venture funding and was valued at more than $8 billion in an April funding round — could eventually sell off parts or all of its business to stay financially stable. As one person close to the matter put it, the scale of the vandalism this year has made clear that change is inevitable.The backlash has been fueled in large part by Wired's own reporting over the past month, which has documented police officers allegedly misusing Flock's system to track former romantic partners and colleagues, found that agencies share access to the network far more widely than expected, raised questions about the opacity of how Flock's devices are manufactured, and detailed just how much data the cameras collect after analyzing a dismantled unit.Flock CEO Garrett Langley addressed the backlash last month on the All-In podcast, acknowledging that the criticism's biggest toll had been on internal morale, and expressing frustration that the company was facing anger online for practices it says it's carried out unchanged for nine years, insisting the goal has always been public safety.The controversy has also drawn attention to how far Flock's technology has expanded beyond its original purpose. Wired reported last month that the company has built AI-powered investigative tools capable of identifying drivers, surfacing potential associates based on movement patterns, and searching across police records and other databases. A separate Wired analysis found software capable of continuously scanning live camera feeds for people matching written physical descriptions, along with signs of potential integrations with drones and other surveillance systems — findings likely to add further fuel to the very backlash the company is now trying to manage.
Article Summary: Flock Safety announced a voluntary separation program, offering a "generous" severance package to employees who choose to leave. The company has seen dozens of cities terminate contracts in recent months, citing privacy concerns and alleged misuse of its technology. Advocacy groups say at least 93 city and county governments cut ties with Flock in August alone.

Article Title: Meta launches fresh legal challenge against UK online safety rules; challenges Ofcom's decision to place WhatsApp and Instagram under Category 1 classification
Article Text:
Meta launches fresh legal challenge against UK online safety rules

Why is Meta challenging Ofcom

Meta faces other legal disputes with Ofcom

UK officials raise concerns over delays

When will the Online Safety Act be fully implemented

Meta says it is challenging implementation, not the law

Meta has started another legal challenge against the UK’s online safety regulator Ofcom, as the company disputes how parts of the country’s Online Safety Act are being applied. The latest case relates to the classification of WhatsApp and Instagram as Category 1 services, which brings additional duties under the law. According a Financial Times report, these include stronger requirements around fraudulent advertising, transparency and the handling of illegal content. Ofcom’s register currently lists both Instagram and WhatsApp as Category 1 services.The latest appeal adds to several legal disputes between Meta and Ofcom as the UK regulator works to implement the Online Safety Act.As per the FT report, Meta is challenging Ofcom’s decision to place WhatsApp and Instagram under the Category 1 classification. Ofcom says Category 1 services are among the most widely used online services and face additional responsibilities under the Online Safety Act. These include greater transparency and accountability, more user controls and measures to protect users from fraudulent advertising.Meta argues that some of the Category 1 duties are not designed for private one-to-one and small-group messaging services. The company is not alone in challenging Ofcom's categorisation decisions.Roblox and Quora are also appealing the regulator's decisions relating to their services.The latest case is not Meta's only legal challenge involving Ofcom. The company is also challenging the regulator over its fees and potential fines under the Online Safety Act. Ofcom's costs for enforcing the rules are recovered through fees paid by certain technology companies, with the amount linked to their qualifying worldwide revenue.Meta has argued that this approach places a disproportionate burden on larger companies because their worldwide revenue is used to calculate the fees.The company has also challenged Ofcom's requests for information from platforms. Meta, along with TikTok and X, has argued that some information requests go beyond what is allowed under the law or what is necessary and proportionate, according to the Financial Times.The legal challenges have raised concerns among some British officials and politicians that court proceedings could slow the implementation of the Online Safety Act. Damian Collins, a former junior minister for technology and the digital economy, said:“It’s clearly a deliberate strategy by Meta to frustrate and delay the implementation of the Online Safety Act. It is a form of lawfare to tie up the regulator. The law is clear and it is what parliament wanted.”He also said large technology companies have “limitless resources” to challenge the regulator and argued that the government should provide Ofcom with more funding.Culture Secretary Lisa Nandy also criticised the pace of enforcement this week, saying: “it has been incredibly slow . . . we want to see Ofcom enforcing the law more robustly and more quickly”. Oliver Griffiths, Ofcom's group director for online safety, said the regulator was “underwhelmed” by progress and was operating in a “highly litigious environment”, according to the Financial Times.The Online Safety Act came into force in stages from April 2025, with different duties being introduced over time. Ofcom's current timetable includes further work on additional safety measures during autumn 2026, while Category 1 and other categorised services face further compliance requirements.Ofcom has said the Category 1 rules cover areas including user empowerment, identity verification, complaints, terms of service, news and journalistic content, and protections for content of democratic importance.Meta said its legal action is not an attempt to challenge the Online Safety Act itself. A Meta spokesperson quoted in the FT report said:“Like many others in the industry, including TikTok, Roblox, X and Quora, we are challenging specific aspects of implementation.” The spokesperson added:“These are not challenges to the law itself, but how Ofcom has interpreted it. This is a normal feature of any new regulatory regime being bedded in and ensures questions of process, scope and implementation get settled so the law is applied proportionately, accurately and consistently.”Ofcom, meanwhile, said it would defend its decisions. An Ofcom spokesperson said:“Parliament has charged us with the job of regulating an industry that has been unregulated and unaccountable for more than 20 years.”The regulator added: “Meta, X and TikTok are challenging our efforts to gather information from them. Meta is challenging us on our ability to set fees and maximum fines. Separately, Roblox, WhatsApp, Instagram and Quora are appealing our decisions in July to designate them as category 1 services. On all these fronts, we will robustly defend our reasoning and decisions.”
Article Summary: Meta has started another legal challenge against the UK's online safety regulator Ofcom. The company disputes how parts of the country's Online Safety Act are being applied. The latest case relates to the classification of WhatsApp and Instagram as Category 1 services, which brings additional duties under the law.

Article Title: Pentagon wants to give its men access to 'military versions' of ChatGPT and Grok, here's what these specialised versions will offer
Article Text:
How ChatGPT and Grok are being added to GenAI.mil

What ChatGPT Mil will offer military users

What the military version of Grok will offer

Why the Pentagon is pushing AI into daily workflows

Why Anthropic’s Claude is missing

Poll Vote & Share your view Do you support the integration of AI tools like ChatGPT and Grok in military operations? Yes, it will improve efficiency No, there are security concerns 3k+ users shared opinion today 5k+ users already voted today 3k+ users shared opinion today Share Opinion

ChatGPT and Grok are coming to the Pentagon’s GenAI.mil platform as the Department of War expands access to specialised AI tools for military personnel and civilian workers. The two systems will be available for handling Controlled Unclassified Information (CUI) at Impact Level 5 (IL5), according to the Pentagon.The Department of War announced Monday that the military versions of ChatGPT and Grok will join GenAI.mil, which launched in December with access only to a specialised version of Google’s Gemini. The department said the platform now has 1.7 million users among its 3 million-strong workforce, including military members and civilians.The move follows contracts worth up to $200 million each that the department awarded to OpenAI and Elon Musk’s SpaceXAI for AI tools. Google and Anthropic also received contracts at the time.ChatGPT Mil is being provided through OpenAI for Government, an initiative launched last summer to bring the company’s AI products to government workers. The Pentagon said the version available through GenAI.mil is designed for its secure environment and tailored to military needs.“ChatGPT on GenAI.mil will make unclassified work throughout the Department more efficient, freeing up time and resources so DoW personnel can focus on the mission,” Joe Larson, vice president and head of government at OpenAI, said in a statement to Fortune.“ChatGPT Mil brings a familiar commercial experience into the Department’s secure environment, tailored to warfighter needs,” the Pentagon said in a press release.ChatGPT Mil will keep data within its environment and will not use it to train its models, the Pentagon said. Service members will be able to use the specialised versions of ChatGPT and Grok for CUI at Impact Level 5.IL5 refers to sensitive US government information that is not classified but requires additional security controls. Much of the military’s work remains unclassified and involves routine, document-heavy tasks in areas such as human resources, logistics and contracting.A person familiar with OpenAI’s uses said these areas could benefit from ChatGPT’s ability to process large amounts of information.The Pentagon’s version of Grok, called Starshield AI’s Grok for Government, will provide access to deep thinking, inference, and different reasoning settings, including auto, fast and expert.The Department of War said the system can support several operational tasks, including market research analysis for acquisition professionals and supply-chain management for logisticians.The department said the technology will enable “the Joint Force to execute missions faster and with greater precision across numerous operational contexts, ranging from market research analysis for acquisition professionals to supply-chain management for logisticians.”The rollout comes as War Secretary Pete Hegseth pushes to make AI part of the Pentagon’s daily work. The effort follows the White House AI Action Plan, which says, “The United States must aggressively adopt AI within its Armed Forces if it is to maintain its global military preeminence.”A War Department official said the military is moving toward an “AI-first” mentality that will change how it fights, thinks and organises.Hegseth had previously instructed department personnel to incorporate AI into their routine work when GenAI.mil launched in December.“I expect every member of the Department to log in, learn it, and incorporate it into your workflows immediately. AI should be in your battle rhythm every single day,” Hegseth wrote in a December memo.Anthropic’s Claude is notably absent from the latest additions. Earlier, the company disputed the Department of War's restrictions on using its technology for autonomous weapons and surveillance.In February, US President Donald Trump directed federal agencies to stop using Anthropic’s technology, while Hegseth said he would designate the company a “supply-chain risk.” Anthropic sued the government a month later.Last week, a judge ruled that the Department of War had acted unlawfully by designating Anthropic a supply-chain risk.
Article Summary: ChatGPT and Grok will be available for handling Controlled Unclassified Information (CUI) at Impact Level 5 (IL5) The Pentagon said the system can support several operational tasks, including market research analysis for acquisition professionals and supply-chain management for logisticians.
